papers.title: Preferences for Accessible Health Information Among Deaf, Blind, and DeafBlind Adults: A Descriptive Qualitative Study
papers.abstract: Overview. People with sensory disabilities (e.g., deaf or hard-of-hearing [DHH], blind/low vision [BLV], and DeafBlind) encounter difficulties when accessing health information. These barriers impede people with sensory disabilities in obtaining, understanding, and using health information. This study aimed to identify barriers, facilitators, and preferred formats for health information to inform inclusive health communication, while addressing the variety of accessibility needs across people who are DHH, BLV, and DeafBlind. Methods. We conducted a qualitative study using eight focus groups and eleven individual interviews with adults with different types of sensory disabilities. Interviews were conducted directly in English or American Sign Language, and recordings were professionally transcribed. Discussions explored experiences accessing health information, information source preferences, accessibility barriers, and reactions to different formats. Transcripts were coded using a hybrid thematic analysis process. Themes were generated through team discussions, code synthesis, and community partner feedback. Results. We developed three themes summarizing user-centered perspectives for designing consumer health information resources. Participants obtained health information from various sources including clinicians, family, friends, internet searches, and ChatGPT. Barriers included information overload, medical jargon, inaccessible website design, and communication breakdowns with clinicians. Preferences for health information formats differed across disability groups. Key recommendations included simplified language, structured layouts, and compatibility with assistive technologies (e.g., screen readers). Conclusion. Despite varying accessibility needs across disabilities, participants agreed health information must be delivered through multiple accessible formats to meet diverse sensory needs. These findings are being used to develop health promotion checklists to enhance accessibility for people with sensory disabilities.

papers.title: REMI: A Free Tool for Truncated Proximity Searching in PubMed
papers.abstract: Background: PubMed is the most comprehensive freely available database for medical and health sciences publications, making it an essential platform for literature searching in budget-constrained settings (e.g. non-academic hospitals). However, unlike subscription platforms (e.g. Ovid MEDLINE), it cannot combine truncation with proximity operators. Searchers must therefore either enumerate every word form manually, risking missed variants, or fall back on Boolean AND, which retrieves many irrelevant records. We developed REMI (Related Expression Machine Identification), a free, open-source web application which emulates truncated proximity searching in PubMed. Case Presentation: REMI was developed at Maastricht University Library. Through the NCBI E-utilities, it identifies the variants of truncated terms that occur in PubMed records. An iterative exclusion procedure, which reruns the search for each concept while excluding that concept's variants already found, surfaces progressively rarer forms. Users select relevant variants from frequency-ranked lists, and REMI combines them into native PubMed proximity clauses that can be documented, peer reviewed, and rerun without REMI. Performance of REMI was evaluated by comparison to four Ovid MEDLINE search strategies from published reviews. REMI's proximity search was able to identify all included articles found with the original Ovid MEDLINE query. Conclusions: REMI makes truncated proximity searching available in PubMed while keeping searches transparent, reliable, and reproducible, which particularly benefits searchers without access to subscription platforms. Because variant discovery is a sampling procedure, completeness is not guaranteed, and long searches require variant selection. Other libraries can use, host, or adapt the tool, however, native support in PubMed would remain the preferable solution.

papers.title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
papers.abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

papers.title: A Blockchain-Enabled Federated Ensemble Framework for Privacy-Preserving Mortality Prediction Across Heterogeneous Healthcare Systems
papers.abstract: Objective: To test whether a smart contract that admits hospital-trained models to a shared mortality model only after peer hospitals verify their performance can exclude poisoned or substituted models, and at what cost. Design: Retrospective simulation study of a federated learning protocol. Methodology: In the Blockchain-Enabled Federated Ensemble (BFE), hospitals committed SHA-256 digests of locally trained XGBoost and random-forest models to a Solidity contract; peers posted digest-bound validation AUROCs, and the contract admitted models with a median peer AUROC of at least 0.70. Admitted models were pooled by weighted logit averaging (BFE-PW) or stacking (BFE-Stack) with federated recalibration. Code and drafts were produced with an AI coding assistant under the authors' supervision. Setting: Four hospitals simulated from one academic centre with age, renal case-mix and laboratory-availability skew; a data-scarce regime keeping 5-20% of each hospital's patients; and a natural partition by care era. Participants: 425,215 adult admissions (186,103 patients; 2.35% in-hospital mortality) in MIMIC-IV v3.1, with predictors from the first 24 hours. Interventions: BFE against centralised, local-only, FedAvg, FedProx, median and Multi-Krum FedAvg and federated logistic regression, under seven attacks on training, attestation, recalibration and model delivery. Main outcome measures: AUROC and AUPRC (joint patient-clustered bootstrap), calibration, attack effects, gas and transactions. Results: Under gross label flipping, FedAvg lost 29% of its AUPRC while the contract excluded the poisoned models in every seed (Multi-Krum FedAvg was equally protected); all substituted models were detected, and collusion blocked release. A targeted flip of female deaths passed the gate and lowered sensitivity for deaths in women from 32.8% to 27.5%; poisoned recalibration inverted BFE-PW (AUROC 0.098) unless a median-of-sites recalibration was used (0.902). With large hospitals, BFE-PW matched FedAvg in AUROC (0.902) and BFE-Stack matched FedProx (0.907 and 0.906), below local-only (0.910) and centralised XGBoost (0.915), with lower AUPRC; with 5% of the data, BFE-PW exceeded local models (0.866 against 0.844). Pooled calibration hid two-fold under-prediction at one hospital (observed-to-expected ratio 2.13), which a local intercept corrected (0.93). One aggregation used 37 transactions and 3.3 million gas, rising roughly quadratically with consortium size. Conclusions: Contract-enforced peer attestation gave auditable, automatic exclusion of grossly poisoned and substituted models at a small accuracy cost, but did not detect attacks that preserve validation discrimination. It is most useful for consortia of small hospitals that need a verifiable record of which models entered a shared tool.

papers.title: Building an Auditable Reference Standard for Clinical Information Extraction from Transesophageal Echocardiography Reports
papers.abstract: Objectives To develop an auditable, two-institution reference standard for intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) reports and evaluate whether reviewer disagreement identifies limitations in the underlying clinical information model. Materials and Methods We selected 300 reports (150 per institution) from 925 at the University of Pennsylvania and University of Washington using random sampling and enrichment for challenging documentation. Four trained abstractors applied a shared 39-variable V1 codebook. Independent paired comparisons included 297 reports; three historical reports contributed only to the final reference standard. Categorical agreement used exact agreement and unweighted Cohen's {kappa}; numeric left-ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) used exact agreement and mean absolute differences. Disagreements underwent structured expert adjudication and reason classification. Additional analyses assessed reviewer-pair, sampling-stratified, and population-weighted agreement. Results Among 11,583 formal reviewer-comparison cells, 10,293 (88.9%) were resolved by reviewer agreement and 1,290 (11.1%) required targeted expert adjudication (1,289 tasks). Codebook/schema ambiguity (40.8%) and interpretation/classification differences (25.2%) together accounted for 66.0% of targeted tasks. Adjudication was concentrated in aortic dissection, valve type, and post-intervention findings. Categorical {kappa} ranged from 0.364 to 0.960 and was inversely correlated with targeted-adjudication burden (Spearman {rho}=-0.884; 95% CI, -0.955 to -0.734). Sampling-weighted {kappa} changed by no more than 0.05 for 32 of 35 categorical variables. Discussion Structured adjudication identified recurring schema and interpretation challenges beyond individual abstraction errors, providing specific targets for information-model refinement. Conclusion As NLP and LLM-based abstraction tools move toward clinical use, the reference standards used to evaluate them require comparably rigorous development, adjudication, and independent validation.

papers.title: Automated Screening for Generalized Anxiety Disorder Using Voice Analysis and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: This study evaluated machine learning models for screening elevated generalized anxiety symptoms from remotely collected neutral read speech in 1,788 adults from Botswana, Ghana, Nigeria, and Tanzania. Elevated symptoms were defined by Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item (GAD-7) questionnaire scores [≥] 5. Nine classifiers were assessed across nine scenarios defined by speech-task configuration (short sentence, long passage, or both tasks) and sex stratification under participant-separated, repeated nested cross-validation (CV). Acoustic-only models used the extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set, and context-augmented models added age, self-reported health, and sex where applicable. With feature selection, the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCROC) was 0.594 for acoustic-only models and 0.699 for context-augmented models, the latter in the female-only combined-task scenario. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) identified fundamental frequency descriptors as prominent acoustic predictors, while health status and age were the leading predictors in context-augmented models. Performance varied across scenarios, and feature selection provided no consistent benefit. Secondary regression poorly estimated continuous symptom severity. These findings indicate limited discrimination from neutral speech acoustics alone and improved performance with participant context, warranting external validation.

papers.title: Simulation and temporal validation of ICU trajectories after stroke: patient condition, transfer readiness and actual ICU exit
papers.abstract: Objective: To describe how intensive care unit (ICU) time is composed after stroke, and to test whether simulating patient condition, transfer readiness and ICU exit separately predicts as accurately as direct models. Materials and Methods: In 6,366 ICU stays for stroke in MIMIC IV, hourly readiness criteria divided ICU hours into organ support needs, stroke specific needs, and time not explained by these needs. An hourly simulator was built on stays up to 2016, frozen, and validated on 2017 to 2019 (n=1,714) and 2020 onwards (n=1,521). The primary measure was the 24 hour alive exit Brier score versus the strongest direct model (gradient boosting). Results: Unexplained time was 34.1% of hours in standard ICUs and 87.6% in neuro intermediate units. 37.8% of stays lost readiness for [≥]6 consecutive hours after first confirmation. The simulator and gradient boosting were indistinguishable (Brier 0.1238 vs 0.1245; difference -0.0007, 95% CI -0.0030 to 0.0016). The simulator was better calibrated at 48 and 72 hours but discriminated less well (C statistic 0.71 vs 0.74 to 0.75). All models overpredicted exit after 2016; the error lay mainly after readiness (median 40 hours simulated vs 68 observed). Discussion: Readiness was not a single event: patients often lost and regained it, and many stayed long after meeting it, especially in neuro intermediate units, which exist for monitoring. Separate modelling did not improve accuracy but placed the post 2016 error after readiness, as the unit mix changed. Conclusion: The simulator matched the strongest direct model while also generating complete trajectories. It needs external validation before any clinical use.

papers.title: ClinDataBench: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in Clinical Trial Analysis Dataset Construction
papers.abstract: A new drug reaches patients only after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has reviewed its trial evidence, which every application carries as analysis datasets in the Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) Analysis Data Model (ADaM) format that programmers derive by hand from raw trial data, a statistical analysis plan (SAP) and dataset specifications. Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) could take over this work, and a slow-changing industry will adopt them only with evidence of what they get right and wrong. However, work on large language models (LLMs) for CDISC data stops short of evaluating a complete, conformant and reproducible package, and the standard validator checks structure rather than whether each value is derived correctly. We introduce ClinDataBench, built on the public CDISC pilot study: an agent receives 22 Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM) domains, the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and specifications, and must deliver 13 Analysis Data Model (ADaM) datasets, Define-XML metadata and a program that rebuilds them offline. Agents run in containers whose only network route is their model API, restricting online access to published reference outputs during execution. A host-only evaluator scores conformance under the Pinnacle 21 Community (P21) validator, selected derivations, clean reconstruction and effort separately. We compare three settings: Base, which submits the agent's first package; Self-Refine, which revises it without external validation feedback; and CRITIC, which revises it with the agent's own validator report. In an exploratory pilot with six models, the three closed models and DeepSeek delivered all 13 datasets in every setting and eleven of their twelve packages rebuilt semantically, while two other open-weight models delivered no complete package. Validator findings ranged from 15 to 64 dataset-rule pairs. Four of six CRITIC workflows had usable validator comparisons, and each reduced its finding count. None reduced its failed derivation count. The package with the fewest findings carried none of the 234 efficacy summary records in the form the specifications define, showing that lower validator finding counts do not necessarily indicate more correct derivations.

papers.title: Patient- and Family-Expressed Needs and Burdens in Kidney-Related Online Discussions in Taiwan: Large Language Model-Based Analysis Across Clinical Contexts
papers.abstract: Introduction: What people with kidney concerns or disease and their families struggle with between visits may not surface in clinic. We mapped the needs and burdens they express online by clinical context and author. Methods: A large language model read all 22,170 posts reached by a chronic kidney disease tag or kidney lexicon on a Taiwanese forum and 3 ask-a-physician services (1995-2026), applying a companion friction framework with kidney-specific fields, author (patient or family) and clinical context. A second vendor re-read 11,010 posts; 2 physicians labelled relevance, author and context in 200. Results: Among 6,023 kidney-related posts, the reproducibly measured fields most often voiced on the forum were information needs (79%), emotional burden (48%), system navigation (34%) and worry about progression (24%). After abnormal tests, 54%-56% of posts quoted a laboratory value, nearly always with a question or stated uncertainty; renal-diet burden peaked with diagnosed disease; caregiver burden rose to 29% of dialysis-or-transplantation forum posts. Family-written posts more often voiced navigation difficulty and caregiver burden. Most fields agreed with the second vendor (kappa 0.65-0.98). On the model's labels, family members wrote 25% of forum posts about kidney concerns and 74% about dialysis or transplantation; on a 139-post sample, physicians' labels gave 47%-48% for dialysis or transplantation (model 71%). Conclusion: Kidney-related posts carry context-specific information needs and emotional and practical burdens, many voiced by relatives. They suggest candidate responses (test-result explanation, diet support, family-directed information and support) that need evaluation. Keywords: chronic kidney disease; dialysis; patient experience; caregivers; social media; large language models

papers.title: Patient-Expressed Needs, Burdens and Barriers in Taiwanese Online Health Discussions: A Taiwan-Contextualized Friction Framework Applied With Large Language Model-Based Social Listening
papers.abstract: Background: Patients' difficulties with illness and care (not understanding a result, distress, daily restrictions, not knowing where to go, family strain) may not surface in clinical encounters or records. Regulatory guidance on patient-focused drug development recognizes social-media listening as a source of patient experience data, but no systematic framework exists for Traditional Chinese discussions in Taiwan, and keyword pipelines measure such content poorly. Objective: To characterize patient-expressed needs, burdens and barriers ("frictions") in Taiwanese online health discussions with an eight-domain, Taiwan-contextualized framework, identify whose frictions they are, and assess how securely each is measured. Methods: From a 13.6-million-unit archive of the PTT forum and three ask-a-physician services, seeded samples of 9,131 pipeline-flagged units and 1,000 unflagged forum articles (10,130 distinct units) were read in full by a large language model under rubrics for relevance, author (patient or family member) and eight domains: information gap, emotional burden, lifestyle burden, medication experience, system navigation, access barrier, caregiver burden and cost burden. Profiles were reported separately for forum articles and physician submissions and checked against a second vendor, two physicians' independent labels of 160 accepted and rejected units, and the archive's keyword pipeline. Results: Among 2,395 model-confirmed forum articles, 83.1% voiced at least one friction: information gap 59.5% (physicians 86%-93%), emotional burden 39.0%, medication experience 24.1%, lifestyle burden 22.2% and system navigation 16.3%; access barrier, caregiver burden and cost burden were each below 7%. Of 3,105 submissions, nearly all were questions and 53.8% also carried a burden. Navigation rarely concerned insurance (9.1%). Family-authored forum articles (14.5%) more often voiced emotional burden (54.9% vs 36.3%), navigation (34.8% vs 13.2%; instrument-dependent) and access barriers (16.4% vs 4.7%), and patient-authored articles lifestyle burden (24.8% vs 6.9%); caregiver burden came with emotional burden in 86.0% of articles voicing it. Emotional and lifestyle burden were commoner in forum articles than submissions under the model, a second vendor and both physicians; medication experience and navigation were instrument-dependent, and physicians disagreed on cost (32% vs 4%). The keyword pipeline had stored its information-gap output for 29.9% of model-confirmed reference-stratum units and over-counted insurance navigation 2.9-fold; its relevance flag was 50.5% precise for forum articles and reached an estimated 42.9% of patient-voice articles. Conclusions: Systematic listening organized Taiwanese patients' and families' online accounts into eight clinically interpretable friction domains, led by the need to understand and by emotional burden, with family-authored posts more often voicing navigation and access difficulty. These expressed concerns may not surface in routine encounters; they identify candidate targets for patient-centred communication and services, which require evaluation. Some domain levels depended on the reader, and keyword pipelines missed or distorted them, so such work needs full-text reading, explicit definitions and clinician checks. Keywords: social media; patient experience data; patient-focused drug development; unmet needs; caregivers; natural language processing; large language models; content analysis; Taiwan; national health insurance

papers.title: Development and Validation of MetaVidence: A No-Code Application for Accessible and Reproducible Meta-analysis
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Meta-analyses are central to evidence-based medicine, but the R packages that implement current methods require programming skills, and most graphical tools cover only a single study design. Here, we aimed to develop and validate a free no-code application that performs the main forms of meta-analysis within a single interface. METHODS: We developed MetaVidence as a Shiny application built on the meta, metafor, netmeta and lme4 packages, which runs in the browser through WebAssembly and is also available as an R package. Agreement with direct package calls was evaluated across effect measures, models, estimators and secondary analyses, and 12 published meta-analyses were reconstructed. Usability was assessed with the System Usability Scale among researchers who had previously conducted a meta-analysis. RESULTS: MetaVidence performs pairwise, single-arm, pre-calculated, network and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis through a three-step workflow of data verification, model specification and results. In three of the five families, multiple outcomes can be analyzed in a single run with the same settings, and every analysis reports the parameters that should be described in the methods section. A total of 6,321 validation checks were performed, and the maximum absolute difference in the reference-dataset comparisons was 3.9x10^(-16). The diagnostic module reproduced the anti-CCP example of the Cochrane Handbook to within 0.0002, and all 12 published meta-analyses were reproduced within half of the last reported digit. Fifty-nine researchers rated MetaVidence with a mean System Usability Scale score of 82.8 (95% CI 76.2-89.5). CONCLUSIONS: MetaVidence integrates the main forms of meta-analysis into a single validated interface that does not require programming. These findings support its use as an accessible and reproducible resource for evidence synthesis, particularly for researchers without programming skills or statistical support.

papers.title: Using a large language model as the primary coder in health content analysis: a verification framework, per-variable reliability and proposed reporting items.
papers.abstract: Objective: To describe and evaluate a framework for using a large language model (LLM) as the primary coder in health content analysis, and to propose reporting items for LLM assisted studies, because no reporting standard exists. Methods: An LLM coded 6,982 Instagram and TikTok posts using a human written, human calibrated instrument. The framework has six components: human authorship of the instrument; two round human calibration; source discipline; quote anchored coding; verification in a representative and an outcome enriched sample, blinded in both directions; and per variable reliability reporting against a prespecified threshold, with the consequence of failure fixed in advance. Agreement was measured with Gwets AC1, prespecified because the outcome distribution was heavily skewed. Results: Agreement between the two human coders on the primary outcome rose from AC1 0.456 to 0.977 after two ambiguous rules were rewritten. LLM human agreement was 0.847 in the representative sample (N = 150) and 0.868 in the enriched sample (N = 50). Five of eight conditional variables fell below the 0.80 threshold and became exploratory: variables asking whether a defined textual feature was present met it, whereas those requiring graded judgement did not. The human coder identified misinformation more often than the LLM, so prevalence estimates are likely underestimates. Agreement on female targeting was lower for self-identified ethnic minority creators (0.744 versus 0.902). Conclusion: LLM coding cannot be computationally reproduced, so its reliability must be shown empirically: per variable agreement with independent human coding, the direction of remaining error, and a prespecified response to shortfall. The authors propose 18 reporting items for LLM assisted content analysis.

papers.title: ADSMoE: A mixture-of-experts-based transformer autoencoder for discovering multimodal Alzheimer's disease subtypes
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity, posing critical challenges for advancing precision medicine. Existing data-driven approaches often rely on modality-specific clustering or predefined biomarker trajectories, limiting their ability to discover disease subtypes from incomplete, heterogeneous real-world data. In this study, we introduce ADSMoE, a mixture-of-experts (MoE)-based multimodal representation learning framework that jointly identifies AD subtypes as latent disease signatures while accommodating incomplete modality combinations. ADSMoE integrates a Fleximodal MoE encoder that accommodates arbitrary combinations of available modalities with a novel subtype-specific MoE decoder to capture complementary disease characteristics through expert specialization. Using data from 5,422 participants across three independent cohorts, we trained ADSMoE on the ADNI cohort and externally validated the identified subtypes in NACC and UKB without model retraining. The proposed ADSMoE identified four AD subtypes with distinct neuroimaging patterns, genetic and proteomic associations, and clinical characteristics. Benchmarking analyses demonstrated robust subtype discovery and strong biological and clinical relevance, while external validation revealed consistent subtype-associated characteristics across independent cohorts. ADSMoE advances AD subtyping by uncovering biologically and clinically meaningful AD heterogeneity from incomplete multimodal data, providing a scalable framework for disease stratification, biomarker discovery, and future precision medicine applications in AD.

papers.title: Prospective prediction of clinical trial outcomes from public evidence
papers.abstract: Predicting clinical trial outcomes requires interpreting biological and clinical evidence in the context of a specific intervention, population and study design. Here we test whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can predict trial outcomes from publicly available evidence. We introduce TrialDossier, which assembles standardized evidence dossiers, and TrialOutlook, which uses these dossiers with GPT-5 to estimate the probability that a trial meets its prespecified primary endpoint. Among 694 ongoing trials with results expected within six months of cohort assembly, 69 outcomes first disclosed after forecast recording had been adjudicated by 20 October 2026. TrialOutlook achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.819 (95% confidence interval, 0.708 to 0.914) and an average precision of 0.860. TrialOutlook correctly identified 27 of 29 failures (93.1%) and incorrectly classified 17 of 40 successes as failures. We further recorded forecasts for 5,809 ongoing trials associated with US-listed companies and established a public benchmark linking archived evidence and fixed forecasts to adjudicated outcomes as they become available.

papers.title: An LLM-assisted Pipeline for Identifying ClinicalTrials.gov Registry Changes and Their Association with Primary Endpoint Positivity
papers.abstract: Registration of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) in a public registry such as ClinicalTrials.gov should minimize the risk of reporting bias. However, records may be modified during a trial and the resulting discrepancies are not always apparent without a detailed examination of all version histories, a process that is cumbersome when performed manually. We developed an automated workflow to investigate whether specific changes to RCT registry entries are associated with primary endpoint positivity. Our pipeline extracts RCT records from ClinicalTrials.gov and systematically detects changes between successive versions using a combination of deterministic textual analysis and large language model (LLM)-assisted classification. We could show a positive association between trial positivity and changes to primary outcomes (OR 1.91; 95% CI 1.48-2.47) as well as to arms and interventions (OR 2.10; 95% CI 1.62-2.73). Associations were weaker when changes occurred exclusively before the primary completion date, pointing to the importance of timing in evaluating potentially consequential modifications to RCT design. Our automated pipeline can enable analysis of trial registration records at scale, facilitating the work of reviewers and meta-scientists to promote research integrity.

papers.title: WakeSentry: real-time awakening detection from single-channel EEG across sleep cohorts and forehead headbands
papers.abstract: Objective/Background: Awakenings after sleep onset are a core measure of sleep continuity, and EEG headbands and closed-loop stimulators, now used at home, must detect each one as it happens, to count it or to stop stimulation. Open sleep stagers match expert scorers, yet have been evaluated only offline over whole nights, so their real-time performance is untested. Patients/Methods: To fill this gap, we developed WakeSentry, which reads only past frontal EEG and learns the moment of waking through an awakening module. We tested it on 1,529 nights from five polysomnography (PSG) cohorts, three clinical, each held out of training, and on 224 headband nights, against GSSC, U-Sleep and YASA. Results: At a matched rate of 0.5 false awakenings per hour, WakeSentry caught more awakenings than GSSC in every cohort and on both headbands. On PSG its sensitivity rose from 63.8% to 70.5%, above U-Sleep and YASA on average. On the headbands it rose from 49.8% to 53.9%, a gain lost without the awakening module. With thresholds preset on the training cohorts, it still outperformed GSSC in six of seven test sets, with at most 0.40 false awakenings per hour. As a replayed stimulator gate, it shortened stimulation during wake in five test sets while staying open for at least 85% of N2 and N3. Conclusions: WakeSentry therefore works in patients and on unseen headbands. It can count awakenings at home and stop stimulation at each one, enabling multi-night monitoring of insomnia and closed-loop stimulation that stops when the sleeper wakes.

papers.title: The Shrinking Grace Period and the Downsizing of Ransomware Victims: Exploitation Timelines and Breach Size Among US Health Care Providers, 2016-2026
papers.abstract: Objectives: To examine how quickly software vulnerabilities are exploited after public disclosure, and whether hacking breaches at US health care providers changed in size after 2021, a period in which earlier studies had found attacks concentrating on large organizations. Methods: Retrospective analysis of public data. We linked the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (1,748 entries) with CVE publication dates to measure time to confirmed exploitation by half-year of publication (2021-2025). We also analyzed 8,029 breach reports submitted to the HHS Office for Civil Rights, focusing on hacking/IT incidents at health care providers. Results: Median time to confirmed exploitation was 24 days for vulnerabilities published from late 2021 to mid 2022, 0 days for those published in the second half of 2022, and 6 days in 2023-2025, with no further shortening across 2023-2025 (P = .40). About a quarter were exploited on or before the day of disclosure. Among provider hacking breaches, the share affecting fewer than 5,000 people fell from 42% in 2016 to 32% in 2022 (trend P = .004) and rose to 46% in 2025 (P < .001). Conclusions: The window between disclosure and exploitation had narrowed to about a week before generative AI was widely available. After 2022, breaches moved toward smaller events, reversing the earlier concentration on large organizations. Defenses that depend on patching speed will not protect small providers.

papers.title: Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo compare the performance and cost of System One models (SOMs) with general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on biomedical tasks and evaluate confidence-based routing. Materials and MethodsWe evaluated three SOMs and three LLMs across seven datasets and eight endpoints covering question answering, error detection, structured extraction, and clinical-note assessment. Outcomes included task-specific performance, recorded inference cost and latency, and confidence calibration. Calibration data determined routing schemes and confidence thresholds to evaluate test predictions, with cost-matched random referral as a comparator. ResultsClaude Opus 5.5 had the highest primary performance on all eight endpoints. The strongest SOM, Jev, had competitive performance with the evaluated LLMs and cost less than 1% of Opus on most datasets. Three selected SOM-to-LLM routes reduced costs by 30.0%-71.7% relative to the receiving LLM, with modest reductions in performance. On one benchmark, SOM-to-SOM routing achieved 91.1% accuracy, compared with 82.3% and 82.2% for the individual models. DiscussionSOMs offered favorable performance-cost tradeoffs for most tasks. The magnitude of the advantages depended on task structure and prompting requirements. Confidence-based routing between SOMs and LLMs can leverage complementary model strengths and offers additional flexibility in performance-cost tradeoffs. The price advantages offered by SOMs can facilitate experimentation and development of workflows. This warrants further evaluation on closed datasets. ConclusionFor biomedical tasks with predefined choices, SOMs represent a competitive stand-alone or first-stage approach.

papers.title: Recording sampling rate as a negative-control exposure for detecting measurement-driven bias in heart-rate-variability-outcome associations: a quantitative bias analysis across ICU waveform databases
papers.abstract: ImportanceHeart-rate variability (HRV) is studied extensively as a prognostic marker in critical illness, yet the electrocardiographic sampling rate at which HRV is computed systematically distorts the resulting values. Whether the associations between HRV and clinical outcomes reported in the literature are partly a consequence of this distortion has not been examined directly. ObjectiveTo evaluate whether between-database differences in native ECG sampling rate can be used as a negative-control exposure to detect measurement-driven bias in HRV-outcome associations, and to quantify the sensitivity of a published association to an empirically measured distortion coefficient using quantitative bias analysis (QBA). DesignA methods investigation in three parts. Part I sets out the causal structure and states why a strict instrumental-variable (IV) design is inappropriate here. Part II derives a bias-correction factor under a multiplicative measurement-error model and propagates the empirical confidence interval of the distortion coefficient as a sensitivity band. Part III applies the procedure to an observed HRV-mortality association from a single ICU waveform database, and examines the separate bias arising from threshold-based categorisation. Setting and data sourcesTwo critical-care waveform databases with different native sampling rates (MIMIC-IV Waveform, approximately 250 Hz; MIMIC-III Waveform Matched p04, 125 Hz) and an independent 500-Hz reference cohort (PTB-XL) for mechanism validation. The outcome association was estimated in 1,445 ICU stays from MIMIC-III p04, of whom 141 died in hospital (9.8%). ExposuresNative ECG sampling rate as a negative-control exposure; SDNN, RMSSD and heart rate as the measured exposures whose associations with mortality are evaluated. Main outcomes and measuresIn-hospital mortality. Distortion coefficients were obtained by end-to-end reprocessing of 7,293 original waveform segments with a fixed QRS detector. Corrected odds ratios were reported as QBA sensitivity bands rather than point-identified effects. Misclassification was quantified as the proportion of recordings below a 20 ms HRV threshold reclassified above it by coarse sampling. ResultsEnd-to-end reprocessing gave an RMSSD distortion coefficient of 1.1575 (95% CI 1.0835-1.2492; 2,276 segments in 188 patients) for 250[->]62.5 Hz and 1.0588 (95% CI 1.0294-1.1033; 4,988 segments) for 125[->]62.5 Hz; high-frequency power was more affected than low-frequency power (1.2033 vs 1.0716). Under the multiplicative model, an observed crude RMSSD-mortality odds ratio of 1.802 corresponded to a corrected interval of 1.8335-1.915 across the coefficients 95% CI. The correction was small relative to confounding: the same association fell to 1.116 after age adjustment. Coarse sampling reclassified 33.70% of low-HRV recordings in MIMIC-IV and 20.72% in MIMIC-III, a larger potential source of bias than the continuous-scale correction. The cross-database negative-control gradient was completed after linking both waveform cohorts to hospital outcomes: RMSSD inflation was reproducible (median x1.101 at 125[->]62.5 Hz in MIMIC-III and x1.270 at 250[->]62.5 Hz in MIMIC-IV), but the age-adjusted HRV-mortality risk ratio did not increase at lower rates (MIMIC-III 1.70[->]1.21; MIMIC-IV 1.31[->]1.29[->]1.20; all 95% CIs crossed 1). The falsification test was therefore negative in these cohorts, and we report it as such rather than as evidence that measurement bias is absent. Conclusions and RelevanceSampling rate is a detectable and correctable source of bias in HRV-outcome research. Recording the sampling rate of each signal, stratifying effects by baseline variability, and reporting a QBA sensitivity band before dichotomising HRV would make published associations more interpretable. The object of inference here is the measurement-error method, not a new clinical biomarker; the proposed reporting steps require no additional data collection.

papers.title: Human-Agentic AI Collaboration Workflow for Trend Analysis of ChatGPT Applications in Healthcare
papers.abstract: BackgroundWith the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong potential to transform healthcare research and practice. However, LLMs are probabilistic and generate inherently variable outputs, which create risk and uncertainty in healthcare applications. Therefore, analyzing the current research landscape of ChatGPT applications is imperative to understand applied techniques and related concerns and to facilitate their practical integration into healthcare information systems. ObjectiveLeveraging LLM-based agentic AI with domain experts to analyze trends in ChatGPT healthcare applications and to examine the collaborative and interpretative capacities of LLM agents in broader contexts beyond narrowly defined topics. MethodsThe review used a systematic search of the PubMed and Web of Science databases, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and focused on ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors. To support the review process, an adaptive, iterative LLM-based agentic AI with a human-in-the-loop mechanism was employed for automated metadata extraction, identification, classification, and knowledge synthesis. The extracted information was subsequently used for temporal and thematic analyses, citation network construction, and main-path analysis. ResultsAcross 192 papers, the review identified 511 ChatGPT application types, 690 concern items, and 368 influence usage factors distinct from traditional IT, achieving a metadata error rate of 1.04%. The human-agentic AI workflow enabled efficient synthesis of contextual information across studies, addressing the growing challenge of timely evidence integration in medical knowledge. The findings provide insights into the evolving trajectories of ChatGPT applications in healthcare and demonstrate the value of an expert-validated human-agentic AI workflow in supporting literature analysis and streamlining review processes. ConclusionThis review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors in healthcare. The study further provides meaningful insights into the operational mechanisms of agentic AI, demonstrating the potential of human-AI collaboration for medical informatics research.

papers.title: Eye-to-Eye: Gaze detection as a proxy for medical doctor behaviour during virtual and in-person appointments
papers.abstract: The gaze direction of the physician during consultations plays an important role in patient satisfaction, with several studies pointing to the positive correlation between the amount of time the physician spends looking at the patient and patient satisfaction. Additionally, the effects of the virtual consultation environment on the gaze behaviour of the doctor have yet to be studied. Therefore, this study aims to assess the impact of the virtual consultation environment by comparing the amount of total time the doctor spends looking at the patient between face-to-face and virtual consultations, as well as the average duration during the consultation and the gaze frequency. The study population consisted of 14 doctors divided between 4 medical specialties: Gynaecology/Obstetrics (4), Neurology (3), Endocrinology (3) and General and Familiar Medicine (4). A low-cost desktop that runs an appearance-based gaze estimation pipeline was implemented in the clinical setup. Each doctor recorded 20 face-to-face consultations and 20 virtual consultations, which were then processed by the pipeline to obtain the percentage of time the doctor spent looking at the patient during the consultation. Overall, we found that doctors look more at the patient in virtual consultations compared to face-to-face consultations, both in total time and average duration during the consultation. Within medical specialties, three out the four specialties involved presented clear tendencies to look more at the patient in virtual consultations when compared to face-to-face consultations.

papers.title: Requirements of a knowledge support tool for self-harm in general practice: a mixed-methods study with patients, carers, and clinicians
papers.abstract: Background General practice has a central role in care following self-harm. However, clinicians frequently report uncertainty about best practice and patients describe poor care. A knowledge support tool is an add-on to electronic health systems that may improve services by providing personalised care information. Aim To understand what general practice clinicians, patients and carers need from a novel knowledge support tool for self-harm. Design and Setting Mixed-methods, using quantitative ratings, focus groups and follow-on interviews with general practice clinicians and patients/carers with lived experience of self-harm. Method Clinicians were recruited through social media and professional networks, and patients/carers through a third-sector organisation. During four focus groups and follow-on interviews, we explored the utility of potential content and functionality of a knowledge support tool. Quantitative utility ratings were summarised descriptively and qualitative data were analysed thematically using the framework method. People with lived/living experience were involved throughout. Results 13 clinicians and 14 patients/carers participated. Requirements of the knowledge support tool were captured across three qualitative themes: facilitating person-centred care, accessibility and usability, and balancing competing priorities of general practice. Across these themes, patients' and carers' needs were centred on promoting compassionate relationships and patient agency. Clinicians shared these needs but balanced them with a need to manage patient expectations and practice defensively under limited resources. Conclusion Our findings inform the core design of a knowledge support tool and suggest that such a tool could support the assessment and management of self-harm in general practice.

papers.title: Microcirculation Mirror: A zero-install browser workstation for hand microvascular anatomy and nailfold capillaroscopy
papers.abstract: BackgroundHand microvasculature is conventionally presented through diagrams, cadaveric atlases and specialized optical instruments, while conventional clinical radiography cannot resolve individual capillary loops (5-15 {micro}m lumen) in vivo, which dominate cutaneous oxygen exchange. MethodsWe present Microcirculation Mirror, a zero-install browser workstation that registers layered hand anatomy to a live 21-landmark pose and couples it to a nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) simulator, a lumped microcirculatory model and an imaging-physics module. The single-file application runs offline on a laptop or, over local HTTPS, on a phone as an installable app. ResultsIts 3D atlas contains 136 named structures per hand in six systems from open Z- Anatomy/BodyParts3D meshes, plus a literature-parameterized capillary layer. The NVC module renders a 200x, 1.2-mm field with six deterministic patterns and quantified density, giant capillaries, avascular width fraction, hemorrhages, tortuosity and ramification. A lumped model reports nine estimates (SIM); a physics module shows that a 10-{micro}m capillary occupies 0.07 of a 150-{micro}m detector pixel; with iodinated contrast it retains {approx}0.016% effective contrast, about 60x below a 1% detection threshold; unenhanced blood is {approx}270x lower. The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms per frame; system merging reduces atlas draw calls from 136 to 6. ConclusionsThe camera-overlay layers are templates, the atlas macro-anatomy is open mesh data, and the capillary layer is sampled. No patient data are used. The instrument is a product prototype, not a medical device, and provides a reproducible framework for making multi-scale microvascular reasoning visible.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes
authors: M. B. van der Hout-van der Jagt
papers.abstract: BackgroundRisk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. MethodsThis secondary analysis included 9,289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-13). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 1-3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported no (low risk), yes (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. FindingsThe adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each womans three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). InterpretationFor fetal growth outcomes, how a womans predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a womans follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit. FundingNone. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed from database inception to Oct 28, 2026, for English-language studies in humans, combining terms for gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction or small for gestational age, and large for gestational age with terms for prediction models and for longitudinal or repeated assessment, risk trajectories, conformal prediction, or predictive uncertainty. We also searched for conformal prediction applied to longitudinal clinical data. Most models predicted a single complication at a fixed gestational age. Longitudinal models updated risk using repeated measurements of blood pressure, biomarkers or fetal biometry, and some showed that changes in these measurements, including fetal growth velocity, improved prediction. We found no study that tested whether a womans earlier predictions add information beyond her most recent prediction. Individual-level uncertainty was rarely quantified in antenatal prediction, and we found no application of conformal prediction in antenatal care. Conformal methods have been used for repeated prediction in other clinical settings, but we found no evaluation of how often prediction sets include the actual outcome across a patients successive predictions.

papers.title: Future-Information Leakage in 30-Day Readmission Prediction: An Empirical Audit and a Calibrated Electronic Health Record Model in Medicare-Insured Adults
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and internally validate a calibrated discharge model of 30-day within-system readmission in Medicare-insured adults, and to quantify how a future-information leak and outcome artifacts distorted performance, timing, and subgroup conclusions. Materials and MethodsRetrospective study of 236,906 Medicare-insured MIMIC-IV v3.1 admissions (87,750 patients; prevalence 21.4%). Predictors were audited for discharge-time availability; history features were tested for future information and recomputed from raw timestamps. A consensus gradient-boosted (XGBoost) model was selected inside patient-grouped folds; CIs used patient-cluster bootstrap. ResultsA feature documented as a prior 180-day length-of-stay trend used each patients whole record, including later admissions; removing it and two derived terms lowered test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 0.774 to 0.706. The corrected procedure reached an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.7057 (95% CI 0.7016 to 0.7102; primary); the 44-feature model scored 0.7056 on the historically exposed test partition (calibration slope 0.99), above reconstructed LACE and HOSPITAL (both P<.001). A day-1 discrimination peak largely reflected 2,368 probable administrative continuations within 1 hour of discharge; merging these into the preceding stay gave test AUROC 0.698 (0.702 after refitting). The White minus Black AUROC difference was 0.003 (95% CI -0.018 to 0.024); specificity was lower for Black patients (0.61 vs 0.69). DiscussionDocumentation audits and patient-grouped validation missed a leak that inflated discrimination and created spurious subgroup and calendar-period differences; simple empirical checks found it. ConclusionEmpirical leakage checks should accompany availability audits. The corrected model is calibrated, moderately discriminating, and needs external validation before clinical use.

papers.title: Effect of Data Preprocessing Decisions on Sepsis-3 Labels in MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD: A Sensitivity Analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectivePublished Sepsis-3 detection rates range from 3.4 % to 65.2 % in MIMIC-III and from 9.8 % to 47.9 % in eICU-CRD. We tested whether data preprocessing decisions alone produce differences of this magnitude when data, cohort and sepsis definition are held fixed. Materials and MethodsUsing the MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD databases we developed and applied a configurable pipeline (medalabel) that stepwise maps the databases into the OMOP Common Data Model, standardizes and cleans the data, and preprocesses them to compute Sepsis-3 labels. Each setting of the preprocessing represents one decision of published Sepsis-3 implementations, and settings can be freely combined. On fixed cohorts of first ICU stays (13,388 in MIMIC-III, 94,782 in eICU-CRD), we changed one setting of a reference configuration at a time (51 variants in five preprocessing domains) and compared detection rates and septic stays (Jaccard index) with the reference. We approximately reconstructed six published pipelines and combined the settings with the largest effects in pairs to test whether their effects add up. The time a value is measured can differ from the time it is documented and thus available for automated analysis. Beyond the usual retrospective view based on measurement time, the pipeline optionally combines both time points to simulate a real-time system. ResultsThe reference configuration labelled 31.5 % of ICU stays in MIMIC-III and 8.2 % in eICU-CRD as septic. Changing a single setting resulted in sepsis detection rates of 15.3-58.6 % in MIMIC-III and 4.6- 17.2 % in eICU-CRD. The largest shifts from the reference, all in the same direction in both databases, came from the SOFA baseline, up to +27.1 percentage points (pp) in MIMIC-III and +9.0 pp in eICU-CRD, from disabling imputation (-16.3 and -2.5 pp), the temporal window (+12.6 and +5.3 pp) and aggregation (-10.1 and -0.8 pp); clinician-validated parameter sets had little effect (-4.8 and -1.1 pp). Even variants that changed the rate by less than 2 pp labelled partly different patients, with Jaccard indices as low as 0.67 in MIMIC-III and 0.56 in eICU-CRD (1 = identical septic stays). Reconstructions deviated from the published rates by 2-10 pp. Two settings applied together deviated from the sum of their single effects by 0.9-11.8 pp in MIMIC-III and by up to 4.9 pp in eICU-CRD. Simulating a real-time system lowered the MIMIC-III rate by 5.0 pp and delayed the label in 45 % of the stays that remained septic. DiscussionWith the infection criterion held fixed, preprocessing decisions alone can produce a considerable part of the variation between published sepsis detection rates. Similar rates can stem from different patients, which makes studies and prediction models difficult to compare, and retrospective labels rely on values that a real-time system would not yet have. ConclusionSepsis-3 labels from health records are only comparable if their data preprocessing is known. Configurable pipelines allow quantifying the effect of these decisions, computing alternative labels on the same data and, in future, validating them against clinician-adjudicated cases.

papers.title: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories
papers.abstract: BackgroundLaboratory medicine underpins clinical decision-making across nearly every care setting. Clinical laboratory errors and delays can compromise diagnostic reliability and patient care. However, laboratory quality and operational data are commonly reviewed through separate manual workflows, limiting timely recognition of emerging problems across complementary data sources. MethodsWe developed and evaluated LabARIA (Laboratory Agentic Reasoning and Integrative Analytics), a multi-agent AI system for coordinated surveillance of specimen workflows, analytical quality control, and laboratory operations. We conducted a single-center retrospective system development and evaluation at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center using laboratory data collected from May 1 through June 18, 2026, including 177,480 specimen-panel records, 75,103 internal quality-control (IQC) measurements, 633 proficiency-testing challenges, and 422 recalibration or maintenance actions. Forecasting agents were evaluated using patient-result streams with controlled perturbations, and synthetic staffing and inventory data. We assessed specimen rejection, cancellation, and turnaround-time patterns; warning recall and lead time before documented laboratory actions; assay-specific patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) performance; and exploratory operational forecasting discrimination. FindingsLabARIA characterized specimen and workflow patterns across clinical units and time periods, including hemolysis-related potassium rejections in the intensive care unit during early morning hours (49 of 367 tests [13.3%]). For analytical quality monitoring, the IQC agent generated warnings before 407 of 422 recorded QC actions (recall, 0.964 [95% CI, 0.942-0.978]), with a median lead time of 5.40 days (95% CI, 3.75-6.07). PBRTQC agent selected different monitoring strategies across 35 analytes. In a separate analysis, adding PBRTQC increased action recall from 0.964 to 0.993 (95% CI, 0.979-0.998). A dashboard presented tiered alerts for human review, and an accompanying chatbot supported interactive exploration of the summaries. For the operational forecasting module, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 7-day inventory and staffing risk forecasting were 0.800 (95% CI, 0.696-0.881) and 0.877 (95% CI, 0.778-0.950), respectively. InterpretationLabARIA demonstrated the feasibility of coordinating laboratory quality surveillance across heterogeneous data sources, providing a foundation for intelligent clinical laboratories. Prospective studies are warranted to determine whether this approach improves monitoring beyond conventional methods, supports laboratory decisions, and benefits patient care without excessive alert burden. FundingNo external funding. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed and arXiv for studies published between Jan 1, 2016, and Nov 1, 2026, without language restrictions, using ("clinical laboratory" OR "clinical laboratories" OR "laboratory medicine") AND ("artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning" OR "large language model" OR "large language models" OR "agentic AI" OR "multi-agent" OR "multiagent" OR "quality control" OR "laboratory operations"). We included studies addressing laboratory quality monitoring or operations and excluded those focused solely on disease diagnosis or treatment selection. Reliable clinical laboratory services are essential to patient care, yet quality and operational surveillance often relies on manual and retrospective review of data distributed across separate systems, placing substantial burdens on laboratory personnel and contributing to reactive responses to emerging problems. Although laboratory automation has advanced, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning applications in clinical laboratories have generally focused on narrowly defined tasks, such as identifying preanalytical errors, supporting test interpretation, and improving test utilization. Existing approaches typically rely on predefined rules, descriptive dashboards, or task-specific analytical models rather than coordinated surveillance across laboratory workflows. We identified no published study that had developed and evaluated an integrated agentic AI system for laboratory-wide quality and operational surveillance. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first study to develop and evaluate a multi-agent AI system for coordinated laboratory-wide quality and operational surveillance. We developed LabARIA to coordinate specialized agents across specimen workflows, analytical quality monitoring, and laboratory operations, integrating their findings into an interactive dashboard with prioritized alerts, supporting measurements, and recommended follow-up checks for laboratory personnel. Rather than providing descriptive summaries alone, the system brings together complementary analytical findings to support the identification and prioritization of emerging concerns. Using real-world clinical laboratory records, we assessed monitoring performance against documented laboratory actions and established quality-control methods, demonstrating early warnings and complementary warning coverage. We also explored operational risk forecasting using synthetic data. Together, these evaluations provide a practical approach for assessing agentic AI in clinical laboratories. Implications of all the available evidenceOur findings suggest that agentic AI could help advance clinical laboratory quality surveillance from fragmented and reactive review toward more coordinated and proactive monitoring. By integrating complementary monitoring functions and presenting prioritized findings with supporting evidence, agentic systems offer a potential approach to helping laboratory personnel identify emerging concerns and focus their investigations. This study advances agentic laboratory surveillance from concept to implementation and evaluation, representing a step toward intelligent clinical laboratories in which AI supports coordinated quality monitoring and human decision-making.

papers.title: Sex and generation shape the genetic architecture of smoking initiation
papers.abstract: The rapidly changing cultural contexts over the past century modified the genetic factors that influence smoking initiation (SI). Using data from nearly seven million respondents, we conducted genome-wide associations study (GWAS) meta-analyses stratified by sex and generation across European, East Asian, African American, and Latino genetic ancestry populations. Sex and generation, but not genetic ancestry, moderate both the SNP-based heritability estimates and associations with individual loci. Specifically, SI is more heritable in females and younger generations. Furthermore, the impact of both discrete policy changes that target smoking and the gradual cultural redefinition of smoking norms across sex and generation are captured within the patterns of cross-trait genetic correlations between SI and extant smoking-relevant phenotypes. Robust cross-ancestry genetic correlations allowed us to meta-analyze the results across subsamples, identifying 1,717 loci associated with SI, including both main and moderated associations for either moderator. Genome-wide heterogeneity analyses identified 45 sex-specific loci and 7 generation-specific loci with distinct associations with SI. Finemapping analyses highlighted 389 and 304 loci with distinct patterns of potential causal variants by sex and generation. Accordingly, sex-and generation-specific macrosocial contexts dynamically influence the genetic architecture of SI, underscoring the need to consider gene-environment interplay for health behaviors as societal norms evolve.

papers.title: Do Rule-Derived Labels Improve Prediction When Reported Labels Are Limited? A Two-Site Machine Learning Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundRule-derived (weak) labels can enlarge a training set when reported labels are scarce. Their value depends on label quality, on how the extra records shift the training distribution, and on whether the comparison accounts for reported labels set aside for tuning or calibration. MethodsWe ran an exploratory label-budget experiment on Escherichia coli urine cultures from two de-identified electronic health record datasets: Stanford ARMD and UT Southwestern ARMD-UTSW. The task was to predict reported non-susceptibility to cefepime, cefoxitin and ceftazidime (Stanford) and to cefepime and ceftazidime (UT Southwestern). Reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of development patients were drawn over five patient-disjoint outer splits. Logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting were trained with reported labels only, or with added rule-derived labels using equal weights, a tuning-selected weight, class-proportion adjustment or prior-probability correction. These were compared with an all-budget reported-only baseline that used every budgeted reported label for training. Stanford used the inferred labels released with the dataset and a feature set including resistance history. UT Southwestern used researcher-derived labels from Stanford rule text, which were not validated for that site, and an age-only primary model. Brier-score differences were assessed with paired patient-cluster bootstrap intervals. ResultsAll rule-derived labels were susceptible. Equal-weight augmentation lowered mean predicted risk well below observed prevalence (for example, Stanford cefepime at the 10% budget: 0.35% versus 4.85%) and had a higher Brier score than the all-budget baseline in every drug, model and budget summary. The tuning-selected weight did not consistently improve on the all-budget baseline. Its median Brier difference was positive in 38 of 40 drug, model and budget summaries. Its paired intervals lay above zero in 100 of 296 Stanford analyses and 31 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses, and below zero in 3 and 5. The tuning set often selected a weight of zero (146 of 296 and 153 of 198 analyses). At UT Southwestern, the age-only models showed little discrimination (median AUROC 0.49 to 0.54), so those comparisons mainly reflect calibration. ConclusionsUnder these designs, rule-derived labels did not consistently improve probability prediction over a reported-only model that used the whole reported-label budget for training. Evaluations of weak supervision should include such a baseline and should report calibration as well as discrimination.

papers.title: BenchmarkHub: an open-source platform for reproducible evaluation of large language models in healthcare
papers.abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are solely judged by their scores on biomedical benchmarks, yet these scores are rarely reproducible since the prompts, inference settings and model builds are seldom reported. We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source platform for auditable evaluation of language and vision-language models for biomedical research. MethodsBenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub. The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records. The platform samples questions with fixed seeds, runs models directly or as tool-using agents in a code sandbox, grades answers with deterministic rules and stores every prompt, reply and tool call. The interface provides a leaderboard to rank performance of the models, allowing model comparison without any preexisting programming knowledge. FindingsWe used BenchmarkHub to evaluate 12 open-weight models in five experiments on 15 biomedical benchmarks (11 text, two multimodal and two computational biology) and two general benchmarks. The pooled accuracy ranged from 46{middle dot}1% (95% CI 43{middle dot}0-49{middle dot}3) to 80{middle dot}9% (78{middle dot}3-83{middle dot}3). Re-grading the responses with simple answer-extraction rules lowered a models accuracy by up to 33{middle dot}1 percentage points leading to a reorder of the leaderboard. Published scores were found for 23 out of the 143 benchmark/model combinations tested. The accuracy measured by BenchmarkHub was lower than in the published results in 19 out of the 23 available comparisons. The effect of four prompting protocols (1: default prompt; 2: asking the model to answer the letter only; 3: extended reasoning; 4: three-shot prompting) changed MEDQA accuracy by up to 11{middle dot}3 points but was not significant after multiple-testing correction with 150 questions. We also tested the impact of ablation on benchmarking using the MMMU benchmark dataset. Removing images lowered the accuracy by 18{middle dot}0 and 19{middle dot}3 points repectively for the two strongest models. Finally, the accuracy of agentic benchmarks using a sandboxed interpreter increased on computational biology tasks by 36-63 points. InterpretationBenchmarking is essential to assess the impact and validity of LLMs for medical applications. BenchmarkHub allows a fair and rigorous comparison of models across established datasets, including the possibility to upload own datasets. The suite includes visual tools to ease model comparison and ranking without any programming knowledge. Self-hosted infrastructure that records every choice and parameter makes benchmark claims checkable without data leaving the institution. FundingEuropean Union EU4Health Programme (JACARDI), Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities-State Research Agency (MCIN/AEI) with FEDER funds, the European Union Recovery and Resilience Facility-NextGenerationEU, and the Instituto de Salud Carlos III. Research in context Evidence before this studyWe searched PubMed, arXiv and Crossref in October, 2026, for articles published from January, 2022, to October, 2026, without language restrictions, using combinations of the terms "large language model", "benchmark", "evaluation", "reproducibility", "prompt sensitivity", "medical", "clinical", "multimodal", "image", "agent" and "bioinformatics". A systematic review of 519 studies found that LLM evaluations in healthcare rely mainly on exam-style questions, rarely use real patient data and seldom report evaluation settings. Holistic frameworks and new task-specific benchmarks, including two published in this journal have broadened what is measured, but headline scores are usually produced by model developers with incompletely described protocols. Studies outside medicine show that prompt format, answer extraction and nominally deterministic decoding can each change benchmark accuracy substantially, and that many questions in general multimodal benchmarks can be answered from the text alone, without looking at the image. Much of this evidence comes from preprints or developer-run evaluations, and we found no medical study that quantified, on the same items and within one framework, the effects of prompting protocol, answer extraction, image availability and tool access, nor an open, self-hosted platform built for that purpose. Added value of this studyBenchmarkHub is, to our knowledge, the first open-source platform that combines a web interface, command-line and REST access, local and cloud model providers, a sandboxed tool-use agent loop, procedurally generated computational biology benchmarks and a complete per-question audit trail. Using only the platform and 12 locally served open-weight models, we show that the answer-extraction rule alone can change medical accuracy by more than the gaps between models and reorder them, that published scores are usually higher than those measured under a documented protocol, that protocol effects need larger samples than are typically used, that on a medical multimodal benchmark the strongest models kept about 90% of their accuracy without the images, and that tool access transforms performance on computational biology tasks. Implications of all the available evidenceMedical benchmark scores should be reported together with the protocol, answer-extraction rules, decoding settings, model build and input modality that produced them, and comparisons between models should be paired and made under identical conditions. Self-hosted evaluation infrastructure allows hospitals and research institutes to do this for their own candidate models without sharing data, as a reproducible screening step that precedes, and does not replace, clinical validation.
